title: Perfect is His way
hook: perfect is His way and perfect His Word (Sukhmani 24)

segments.voice: Yesterday, ashtpadi 24, and your line: the perfect one. Did a habitual perfect remind you of anything? The salok rang pooraa four times. Today: what does a perfect way look like on a day that isn't? Day five hundred thirty-one.

The car won't start. The rain comes in sideways. The email you were waiting for says no. By ten in the morning the day is clearly not going to be a perfect one, and you can feel the whole thing tilting. Then Sukhmani's last ashtpadi says something that sounds almost cheeky on a day like that: perfect is His way, and perfect His Word. It isn't saying the car will start. It's saying something about what lies underneath the day that won't.
screen: `THE CAR WON'T START.` → `THE EMAIL SAYS NO.` → `PERFECT, UNDERNEATH?`

segments.voice: The twenty-fourth ashtpadi keeps ringing the word pooraa, perfect, through its stanzas. Its first stanza begins, in paraphrase: listen to the teaching of the perfect Guru; see the Supreme as near you; remember God with every breath, and the anxiety of the mind will lift. Perfect Guru, perfect Word, perfect way. Now, here's what perfect is not claiming. It isn't claiming that every day will feel perfect, or that bad things don't happen. Sikh history has martyrdoms in it, two Gurus among them. Nobody in this tradition pretends life is smooth. What it claims is something underneath the surface of the day: that God's hukam, God's order, is whole, even when we only see a ragged piece of it. Sikhs have a word for meeting the day that way: bhaanaa, God's will, accepted. Guru Arjan, who wrote Sukhmani, sings in another hymn, in paraphrase: whatever You do seems sweet to me. Sikh tradition remembers that he lived those words to the end. That's the kind of trust this stanza points to. Not pretending the rain isn't sideways. Trusting there's a whole beneath the part. And notice the practical line in the middle: remember God with every breath, and the anxiety lifts. Saas saas. The trust isn't a big leap made once. It's breath by breath, on the imperfect day itself. Perfect, underneath; imperfect, on top. Sukhmani asks the reciter to live in both.
screen: `THE PERFECT GURU, THE PERFECT WORD.` · `NOT A CLAIM THAT DAYS FEEL PERFECT.` · `BHAANAA: GOD'S WILL, ACCEPTED.` · `SAAS SAAS: BREATH BY BREATH.` · then, large: `PERFECT, UNDERNEATH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: trust one imperfect day. Bring to mind what's gone wrong today, or this week. Name it plainly to yourself. Don't argue with it. Then, on each breath in, hold the thought: this is the surface. On each breath out: there's a whole underneath. Breath by breath, like the stanza says. You don't have to feel the trust. Just practice it. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath. The bell holds the time.
Perfect is His way. Sukhmani says God's order and Word are whole even when our day isn't; Sikhs meet it with bhaanaa, trust in God's will, breath by breath.
Your line: perfect, underneath. Today, when something goes wrong, take one slow breath before reacting, and say the line silently. Day five hundred thirty-one.

howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib's last ashtpadi hear of the perfect Guru, Word and way, and meet hard days with bhaanaa, acceptance of God's will, remembering God with each breath.

original.note: Gurmukhi: bhaanaa, God's will, and the Sikh ideal of accepting it.

trapdoor: what you thought: perfect is his way means everything that happens is good.
what it means: God's order is whole underneath, even when the day isn't, and Sikhs practice trust in it breath by breath.
what a scholar hears: Sikh tradition holds up Guru Arjan, Sukhmani's author, as one who lived his line that God's doing seems sweet through his own martyrdom.
